title: Morphology-Guided Deterministic Fabrication of Low-Noise High-Temperature Superconducting Quantum Interference Devices
authors: Bingke Xiang, Wanjuan Tang, Shiqun Liu, Lingtong Hou, Geming Zhang, Yibo Wang, Ruonan Wang, Zhiqiang Cao, Jiaqi Wei, Xueshen Wang, Xueying Zhang, Xiaoyang Lin
abstract: Reproducible bicrystal high-temperature superconducting quantum interference devices remain limited by local variability along the grain boundaries that form the Josephson junctions. Here, we develop a site-selective fabrication workflow in which atomic force microscopy maps the intended junction region before lithography, quantifies an apparent grain-boundary width, rejects pore-rich segments, and writes a nearby registration mark for site-specific pattern alignment. The apparent grain-boundary width provides a practical morphology metric, with narrower regions consistently yielding larger critical currents and characteristic voltages. Iterative optimization within this workflow further improves junction and device performance, reaching a liquid-nitrogen-temperature field-noise level of 40 fT Hz^(-1/2). This strategy turns local grain-boundary heterogeneity from an uncontrolled source of variability into a basis for site-selective fabrication, providing a route towards scalable manufacturing of low-noise HTS SQUIDs with high uniformity.
summary: The research addresses variability in HTS SQUIDs by developing a novel fabrication workflow that uses AFM imaging to map grain boundary morphology. By quantifying the apparent width ($	ext{w}_{	ext{AFM}}$), the authors demonstrate that selecting narrower regions significantly boosts critical current and reduces noise, turning material heterogeneity into a controllable design parameter for scalable superconducting devices.
main_problem: Reproducible fabrication of low-noise High-Temperature Superconducting (HTS) Quantum Interference Devices (SQUIDs) is severely limited by local variability along the grain boundaries forming Josephson junctions.
main_result: The authors developed an AFM-guided workflow showing that junction critical current ($I_c$) strongly correlates with a measured apparent grain-boundary width ($	ext{w}_{	ext{AFM}}$), allowing for site-selective fabrication to achieve low noise levels (40 fT Hz^(-1/2)).
method: The methodology involves using Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) *before* lithography to map the local morphology of grain boundaries, quantifying an apparent width ($	ext{w}_{	ext{AFM}}$), and then using this metric for site selection.
model_or_system: The physical system is HTS thin films deposited on bicrystal substrates, where Josephson junctions are formed across natural grain boundaries. Performance is characterized by electrical measurements like $I$-$V$ curves and SQUID noise spectra.
key_observables: Critical Current ($I_c$), Normal-state Resistance ($R_n$), Apparent Grain-Boundary Width ($	ext{w}_{	ext{AFM}}$), and SQUID Noise Level (e.g., 40 fT Hz^(-1/2)).
important_parameters: Liquid-nitrogen temperature, $	ext{w}_{	ext{AFM}} \approx 40 	ext{ nm}$ (optimal width for high $I_c$).
main_assumptions: The apparent grain-boundary width ($	ext{w}_{	ext{AFM}}$) is treated as a practical, operational process-control metric rather than a direct measure of the microscopic weak-link barrier thickness.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the AFM guidance process (Fig. 1), quantification of boundary widths from topography profiles (Fig. 2), correlation between $I_c$ and $	ext{w}_{	ext{AFM}}$ (Fig. 3), and noise/critical current modulation due to local heterogeneity (Fig. 4).
paper_structure: The paper details the problem of variability in HTS SQUIDs, introduces the AFM-guided site-selective fabrication workflow, presents quantitative analysis showing $I_c$ dependence on $	ext{w}_{	ext{AFM}}$, and concludes with low-noise measurements demonstrating improved uniformity.
why_interesting: This work bridges materials science characterization (AFM morphology) directly into device performance optimization for superconducting circuits, which is highly relevant to understanding disorder effects in correlated superconductors.

Figure 2: AFM-resolved grain-boundary heterogeneity and local alignment mark. a, AFM topography of a pore-rich bicrystal grain boundary (GB). Figure 3: Systematic variation of Josephson junction transport with AFM-resolved grain-boundary width. a, Current–voltage characteristics of bicrystal Josephson junction devices D1–D5. b–d, Critical current, Ic (b), normal-state resistance, Rn (c), and characteristic voltage, IcRn (d), plotted against the AFM-resolved grain- boundary width, wAFM. Ic decreases markedly with increasing wAFM, whereas Rn exhibits a comparatively weaker width dependence. Colors identify the same devices across all panels, with corresponding symbol shapes used in b–d. Horizontal error bars indicate the standard errors of the fitted AFM-derived width.

Figure 4: Signatures of local grain-boundary heterogeneity in Josephson transport and SQUID noise. a, Normalized resistance as a function of temperature for three bicrystal Josephson junctions (J1–J3), vertically offset for clarity. The junctions exhibit distinct transition broadening and resistive tails. b, Normalized effective critical current Ic(B) extracted from resistively shunted junction (RSJ) fits. Traces are vertically offset.
